title: Roblox Game Coding
blurb: Learn Luau and build real Roblox games: parts, events, leaderboards, tweens, RemoteEvents and saving data, all in a live 3D world.

lessons.title: How Roblox games are made
lessons.html:
Every Roblox game, from a simple obby to a giant simulator, is built in Roblox Studio. Studio is a free program where you place 3D objects and write scripts that make them do things.

Scripts in Roblox are written in Luau (say "loo-wow"). Luau is Roblox's version of a language called Lua. It's small, fast and friendly to beginners, which is why so many people learn to code by making Roblox games.

Everything is an Instance

In Roblox, every object in your game is an Instance: a part, a player, a sound, a light, even a script. Instances are arranged in a tree, like folders on a computer. The top of the tree is called game.

Container What goes in it
Workspace Everything you can see in the 3D world: parts, models, the baseplate
Players One Player object for each person in the game
ServerScriptService Scripts that run on the server (the game's "brain")
ReplicatedStorage Things both the server and players' devices can use
StarterPlayer / StarterGui Things copied to each player when they join

Explorer and Properties

Studio has two windows you'll use all the time:

  • Explorer shows the tree of every Instance in your game.
  • Properties shows the settings of whatever you click, like a part's Color, Size and Position.

Scripts do the same thing you'd do by hand in those windows: create Instances and change their properties. The difference is that a script can do it while the game is running, in response to players.

🛠 In Roblox Studio: set up your first place

  1. Download Roblox Studio from create.roblox.com and sign in with your Roblox account.
  2. Click New, then open the Baseplate template.
  3. Open the View tab and turn on Explorer, Properties and Output.
  4. In the Explorer, hover over ServerScriptService, click the + button and choose Script.
  5. Press Play (or F5). Anything your script prints shows up in the Output window.

The simulator in this course

You don't need Studio to start. Every Try it box in these lessons runs real Luau code in a mini Roblox world inside your browser. It has a baseplate, a spawn point and a blocky player you can walk around with W A S D and Space.

Click 🗂 Explorer above any game view to see the same Instance tree Studio shows you. Try it now: press Run, then open the Explorer.

print("Hello from the server!")
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Name = "MyFirstPart"
part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255)
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

quizzes.why: Parts, models and the baseplate all live in `Workspace`. If an Instance is not inside Workspace, it is not drawn in the world.

lessons.title: print, comments and the Output window
lessons.html:
The first thing every programmer learns is how to make the computer show a message. In Luau, that's print. Whatever you print appears in the Output window.

print("Hello, Roblox!")
print("I can print numbers too:", 42)
print(10 + 5)

A few things to notice:

  • Text goes inside quote marks: "like this". Text in code is called a string.
  • You can give print several values separated by commas. It puts a space between them.
  • print(10 + 5) shows 15, because Luau does the math first.

Comments

Anything after two dashes -- is a comment. Luau ignores it. Comments are notes for humans, like you next week.

-- This line is a comment, so it does nothing
print("This runs") -- you can put comments at the end of a line too

--[[
  Two dashes plus two square brackets
  start a comment that covers many lines.
]]

Reading errors

Everyone writes code with mistakes. When Luau can't run your code, Output shows a red error with the script's name and a line number:

ServerScriptService.Script:2: attempt to call a nil value (global 'Print')

This one means line 2 used Print, which doesn't exist. Luau is case-sensitive: print and Print are different names. Run this, read the error, then fix it:

print("Line one works")
Print("Line two has a capital P")
print("Do I run?")

Notice that nothing after the error runs. A script stops at its first error.

lessons.title: Your first Part
lessons.html:
Let's make something appear in the world. Creating an object takes three steps:

  1. Create it with Instance.new("ClassName").
  2. Set its properties, like Size, Color and Position.
  3. Parent it to workspace so it shows up.
local block = Instance.new("Part")   -- 1. create a Part
block.Name = "Box"                   -- 2. set properties
block.Size = Vector3.new(6, 2, 4)
block.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 170, 0)
block.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
block.Parent = workspace             -- 3. put it in the world

Press Run and watch closely. The box falls, because new parts aren't anchored. Roblox physics pulls them down with gravity until they land on something.

Anchored

Set Anchored to true and the part stays exactly where you put it. Floors, walls and obby platforms are almost always anchored.

local platform = Instance.new("Part")
platform.Name = "FloatingPlatform"
platform.Size = Vector3.new(10, 1, 10)
platform.Position = Vector3.new(0, 8, 0)
platform.Anchored = true
platform.Parent = workspace
print("Anchored?", platform.Anchored)

What is local?

local block = ... creates a variable named block that remembers the new part, so the next lines can change it. You'll learn all about variables in Unit 2.

Why parent last?

You can set Parent any time, but setting it last is a good habit. The part shows up already finished instead of popping in and then changing.

🛠 In Roblox Studio: make a part without code

  1. On the Home tab, click Part. A gray block appears.
  2. In Properties, change Color, Size and Position and watch it update.
  3. Tick Anchored so it doesn't fall when you press Play.
  4. Rename it by double-clicking its name in the Explorer.

quizzes.q: You create a Part but forget `part.Parent = workspace`. What happens?
choices: It exists, but nobody can see it in the world
quizzes.why: An Instance with no parent exists in memory, but only things inside Workspace are drawn in the 3D world.

quizzes.q: Why does a new Part fall when the game runs?
choices: Parts are unanchored by default, so gravity pulls them
quizzes.why: New parts have `Anchored = false`. Set `Anchored = true` to freeze a part in place.

choices: Any object in a Roblox game: parts, players, scripts, sounds and more

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.html:
A variable is a name that holds a value so you can use it later. In Luau you create one with local:

local playerName = "Noob123"
local coins = 250
local speed = 16.5
local isVip = false

print(playerName, "has", coins, "coins")

local means the variable belongs to this script (or the block it's in). Always use local when you create a variable. It's faster and avoids bugs.

The basic types

Type Examples Used for
number 5, -3, 16.5 Coins, health, speed. Luau has one number type for whole numbers and decimals.
string "hello", 'Bob' Names and messages. Use double or single quotes.
boolean true, false Yes/no facts, like "is the door open?"
nil nil "Nothing here." A variable with no value is nil.

You can ask Luau for a value's type with type(). For Roblox objects, typeof() gives the exact kind, like "Vector3" or "Instance".

local health = 100
local nothing
print(type(health), type("hi"), type(true), type(nothing))
print(typeof(Vector3.new(1, 2, 3)))

Changing a variable

Use = again (without local) to give a variable a new value:

local lives = 3
print("Lives:", lives)
lives = lives - 1
print("Lives:", lives)
lives -= 1   -- shortcut for lives = lives - 1
print("Lives:", lives)

Luau has shortcut operators: +=, -=, *=, /= and ..=. There is no ++, so write count += 1.

Naming rules

Names can use letters, digits and _, but they can't start with a digit. Roblox programmers usually use camelCase like jumpPower and playerName. Pick names that explain the value: walkSpeed beats ws.

quizzes.q: What is the value of a variable that was declared but never given a value?
quizzes.why: `local x` with no `=` makes `x` equal `nil`, which means "no value".

quizzes.q: Which line adds 5 to `score`?
quizzes.why: `score += 5` is short for `score = score + 5`. Luau has no `++` operator.

lessons.title: Math and strings
lessons.html:
Math operators

Operator Meaning Example Result
+ - * add, subtract, multiply 4 * 3 12
/ divide 7 / 2 3.5
// floor divide (round down) 7 // 2 3
% remainder 7 % 2 1
^ power 2 ^ 5 32 
local coins = 250
local price = 75
print("Can buy:", coins // price)
print("Left over:", coins % price)
print("Area:", 4 ^ 2)

Joining strings with ..

To glue text together, Luau uses two dots .., not +. Numbers are turned into text automatically:

local name = "Ada"
local level = 7
print("Player " .. name .. " is level " .. level)

Using + on text is a common mistake. "Score: " + 10 gives an error, because Luau tries to do math with the word "Score".

String interpolation

Backtick strings let you drop values straight into text with {}. Many Roblox programmers find this the easiest way to build messages:

local name = "Ada"
local coins = 120
print(`{name} has {coins} coins`)
print(`Next level in {500 - coins} coins`)

Handy string tools

local msg = "Hello, Roblox"
print(#msg)                 -- length: 13
print(string.upper(msg))    -- HELLO, ROBLOX
print(msg:lower())          -- same idea using a method: hello, roblox
print(msg:sub(1, 5))        -- characters 1 to 5: Hello
print(string.rep("ha", 3))  -- hahaha
print(tostring(99) .. "!")  -- number to string
print(tonumber("42") + 1)   -- string to number: 43

In Luau, strings count from 1, not 0. msg:sub(1, 5) is the first five characters.

quizzes.q: What is `17 % 5`?
quizzes.why: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with **2 left over**. `%` gives the remainder.

lessons.title: The math library and random numbers
lessons.html:
Luau comes with a math library full of useful tools:

print(math.floor(3.7))        -- round down: 3
print(math.ceil(3.2))         -- round up: 4
print(math.round(3.5))        -- nearest: 4
print(math.abs(-12))          -- distance from zero: 12
print(math.max(4, 9, 2))      -- biggest: 9
print(math.min(4, 9, 2))      -- smallest: 2
print(math.clamp(150, 0, 100))-- keep between 0 and 100: 100
print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi)

math.clamp is great for games. Health should never go above the max or below 0, so math.clamp(health, 0, 100) keeps it in range.

Random numbers

math.random(a, b) picks a whole number from a to b, including both. Games use randomness for loot, spawn points and colors.

local crate = Instance.new("Part")
crate.Name = "Crate"
crate.Size = Vector3.new(3, 3, 3)
crate.Color = Color3.fromRGB(150, 100, 50)
crate.Position = Vector3.new(math.random(-20, 20), 10, math.random(-10, 10))
crate.Parent = workspace
print("Crate dropped at", crate.Position)

Run it a few times: the crate lands somewhere different each time. math.random() with no arguments gives a decimal between 0 and 1, which is handy for chances: if math.random() < 0.1 then means "10% of the time".

lessons.title: Position, Size and Vector3
lessons.html:
Roblox measures distance in studs. A default player is about 5 studs tall. Positions and sizes are written as a Vector3: three numbers for X, Y and Z.

  • X is left and right.
  • Y is up and down. Bigger Y means higher.
  • Z is forward and backward.
local tower = Instance.new("Part")
tower.Name = "Tower"
tower.Size = Vector3.new(4, 20, 4)       -- 4 wide, 20 tall, 4 deep
tower.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)  -- the CENTER of the part
tower.Anchored = true
tower.Parent = workspace

print("Tower is", tower.Size.Y, "studs tall")
print("Top of tower:", tower.Position.Y + tower.Size.Y / 2)

Position is the center of the part. The baseplate's top is at Y = 0, so a 20-tall part needs Y = 10 to sit exactly on the ground.

Vector3 math

You can add and multiply Vector3s, and read .X, .Y, .Z and .Magnitude (length):

local a = Vector3.new(1, 2, 3)
local b = Vector3.new(10, 0, 0)
print(a + b)            -- 11, 2, 3
print(a * 2)            -- 2, 4, 6
print((b - a).Magnitude) -- distance between the two points

Vector3s can't be changed piece by piece. part.Position.Y = 10 gives an error. Build a new one instead:

part.Position = Vector3.new(part.Position.X, 10, part.Position.Z)
part.Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)   -- move up 5 studs

🛠 In Roblox Studio: move parts precisely

  1. Select a part and use the Move, Scale and Rotate tools on the Home tab.
  2. Or type exact numbers into Position and Size in Properties.
  3. In the Model tab, set the move snap (for example 1 stud) so parts line up neatly.

lessons.title: Colors, materials and shapes
lessons.html:
Color3

Colors are Color3 values. There are three ways to make one:

local function block(x, color)
    local p = Instance.new("Part")
    p.Size = Vector3.new(4, 4, 4)
    p.Position = Vector3.new(x, 2, 0)
    p.Anchored = true
    p.Color = color
    p.Parent = workspace
end

block(-10, Color3.new(1, 0, 0))              -- 0 to 1 for red, green, blue
block(-5, Color3.fromRGB(255, 170, 0))       -- 0 to 255, like an art program
block(0, Color3.fromHSV(0.6, 0.8, 1))        -- hue, saturation, brightness
block(5, BrickColor.new("Lime green").Color) -- a named Roblox color

(Don't worry about the local function part yet; it's a shortcut so we don't repeat ourselves. Functions come in Unit 6.)

Color3.fromRGB is usually the easiest: copy the numbers from any color picker. Parts also have a BrickColor property that takes a BrickColor, not a Color3. Mixing them up gives an error like "BrickColor expected, got Color3".

Material, Transparency and Shape

These properties use Enums: fixed lists of choices written as Enum.ListName.Choice.

local orb = Instance.new("Part")
orb.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
orb.Size = Vector3.new(5, 5, 5)
orb.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
orb.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 255)
orb.Position = Vector3.new(0, 6, 0)
orb.Anchored = true
orb.Parent = workspace

local glass = Instance.new("Part")
glass.Size = Vector3.new(10, 8, 1)
glass.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, -6)
glass.Material = Enum.Material.Glass
glass.Transparency = 0.5      -- 0 = solid, 1 = invisible
glass.Anchored = true
glass.Parent = workspace

local pillar = Instance.new("Part")
pillar.Shape = Enum.PartType.Cylinder
pillar.Size = Vector3.new(8, 3, 3)   -- a cylinder's length runs along X
pillar.Position = Vector3.new(10, 1.5, 0)
pillar.Anchored = true
pillar.Parent = workspace

Some other useful properties: CanCollide (can players walk through it?), CanTouch (does it fire Touched events?) and Reflectance.

lessons.title: Finding, cloning and destroying
lessons.html:
Getting objects that already exist

If a part named Door is in workspace, you can reach it with a dot: workspace.Door. But if it doesn't exist, that line errors. FindFirstChild is safer: it returns the child, or nil if there isn't one.

local d = Instance.new("Part") d.Name = "Door" d.Size = Vector3.new(6, 8, 1) d.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, 0) d.Anchored = true d.Color = Color3.fromRGB(120, 80, 40) d.Parent = workspace

local door = workspace.Door              -- fine, because Door exists
door.Color = Color3.fromRGB(200, 40, 40)

local gate = workspace:FindFirstChild("Gate")  -- no Gate, so this is nil
print("Gate is", gate)

-- workspace.Gate would crash with: Gate is not a valid member of Workspace

Dots and colons

  • A dot reads a property or a child: part.Color, workspace.Door.
  • A colon calls a method, which is an action the object can do: part:Destroy(), workspace:FindFirstChild("Door").

Useful methods

Method What it does
:FindFirstChild("Name") Returns the child with that name, or nil
:WaitForChild("Name") Waits until the child exists, then returns it
:GetChildren() Returns a list of all children
:Clone() Makes a copy (set the copy's Parent to show it)
:Destroy() Deletes it forever
:IsA("BasePart") Checks what kind of object it is 
local d = Instance.new("Part") d.Name = "Coin" d.Shape = Enum.PartType.Cylinder d.Size = Vector3.new(0.5, 3, 3) d.Position = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0) d.Anchored = true d.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 0) d.Material = Enum.Material.Neon d.Parent = workspace

local coin = workspace.Coin
local copy = coin:Clone()
copy.Position = coin.Position + Vector3.new(6, 0, 0)
copy.Parent = workspace

task.wait(2)       -- pause for 2 seconds (more about this in Unit 5)
coin:Destroy()
print("Original coin destroyed. The copy is still there.")

🛠 In Roblox Studio: find objects from a script

  1. Put your script inside a part. In the script, script.Parent is that part.
  2. Use workspace:WaitForChild("Name") in scripts that run on players' devices, because things may still be loading.
  3. Right-click any object and choose Copy Path to get the exact path to type.

lessons.title: Comparisons and if statements
lessons.html:
Games are full of decisions: Did the player touch lava? Do they have enough coins? An if statement runs code only when a condition is true.

local coins = 120
local price = 100

if coins >= price then
    print("Purchase complete!")
    coins -= price
end
print("Coins left:", coins)

The shape is always if condition then ... end. Indent the lines inside (press Tab) so you can see what belongs to the if.

Comparison operators

Operator Means
== equal to
~= not equal to (Luau uses ~=, not !=)
< > less than, greater than
<= >= at most, at least

One = stores a value. Two == compare values. if x = 5 then is an error.

else and elseif

local health = 35

if health > 70 then
    print("Feeling great")
elseif health > 30 then
    print("Ouch, find a medkit")
else
    print("Danger!")
end

Luau checks from the top and runs only the first branch that's true. In Luau, elseif is one word.

    print("No lava in this map")
end

When you just need to pick between two values, Luau has a one-line if-expression:

local score = 72
local result = if score >= 60 then "pass" else "try again"

lessons.title: while loops and task.wait
lessons.html:
A loop repeats code. A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is true:

local countdown = 5
while countdown > 0 do
    print(countdown)
    countdown -= 1
    task.wait(1)   -- pause for 1 second
end
print("Go!")

task.wait(seconds) pauses this script without freezing the rest of the game. Run the example and watch the numbers appear one second apart.

Game loops: while true do

Many Roblox scripts have a loop that runs forever, like a light that keeps blinking:

local light = Instance.new("Part")
light.Name = "Siren"
light.Size = Vector3.new(3, 3, 3)
light.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, 0)
light.Anchored = true
light.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
light.Parent = workspace

while true do
    light.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
    task.wait(0.5)
    light.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 80, 255)
    task.wait(0.5)
end

Never forget task.wait!

A while true do loop without a wait never lets anything else happen. The game freezes, and Roblox stops the script with "Script timeout: exhausted allowed execution time". Try it, then add task.wait() to fix it:

local n = 0
while true do
    n += 1
end

task.wait() with no number waits one frame (about 1/60 of a second). That's enough to keep the game running.

You may see old code use wait() instead of task.wait(). They do the same job, but task.wait() is the newer, more accurate version, so use it in new code.

lessons.title: for loops
lessons.html:
When you know how many times to repeat, use a numeric for loop:

for i = 1, 5 do
    print("Lap", i)
end

i starts at 1 and goes up to 5, including 5. You can add a third number, the step:

for i = 0, 20, 5 do print(i) end      -- 0 5 10 15 20
for i = 3, 1, -1 do print(i) end      -- 3 2 1 (count down with a negative step)

Building with loops

Loops are how you build lots of parts without copy-pasting. Here's a staircase. Each step is 1 stud higher and 2 studs further than the last:

for i = 1, 12 do
    local step = Instance.new("Part")
    step.Name = "Step" .. i
    step.Size = Vector3.new(6, 1, 2)
    step.Position = Vector3.new(0, i, -i * 2)
    step.Anchored = true
    step.Color = Color3.fromHSV(i / 12, 0.7, 1)
    step.Parent = workspace
end

Walk your character up the stairs! Notice how i is used in the name, the position and the color.

Loops inside loops

Put one loop inside another to make a grid:

for x = 1, 6 do
    for z = 1, 6 do
        local tile = Instance.new("Part")
        tile.Size = Vector3.new(3.8, 1, 3.8)
        tile.Position = Vector3.new(x * 4 - 14, 0.5, z * 4 - 14)
        tile.Anchored = true
        tile.Color = if (x + z) % 2 == 0 then Color3.new(1, 1, 1) else Color3.new(0.1, 0.1, 0.1)
        tile.Parent = workspace
    end
end

lessons.title: repeat, break and continue
lessons.html:
repeat ... until

A repeat loop runs its body first, then checks the condition. It always runs at least once, and it stops when the condition becomes true:

local roll
repeat
    roll = math.random(1, 6)
    print("Rolled", roll)
until roll == 6
print("Got a six!")

break and continue

  • break leaves a loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this time around and jumps to the next one.
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i % 2 == 0 then
        continue  -- skip even numbers
    end
    if i > 7 then
        break     -- stop completely after 7
    end
    print(i)
end

Timers with loops

Lots of games have a round timer. A for loop counting down with task.wait(1) is all you need:

local sign = Instance.new("Part")
sign.Name = "TimerBlock"
sign.Size = Vector3.new(6, 6, 1)
sign.Position = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0)
sign.Anchored = true
sign.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
sign.Parent = workspace

for secondsLeft = 5, 1, -1 do
    print("Round ends in", secondsLeft)
    sign.Color = Color3.fromHSV(secondsLeft / 15, 1, 1)
    task.wait(1)
end
print("Round over!")
sign.Color = Color3.new(0.3, 0.3, 0.3)

lessons.title: Writing functions
lessons.html:
A function is a named chunk of code you can run whenever you want. You define it once and call it as many times as you like.

local function greet(name)
    print("Welcome to the game, " .. name .. "!")
end

greet("Ada")
greet("Builderman")
  • name is a parameter: a variable that gets its value when the function is called.
  • "Ada" is the argument: the actual value passed in.

return

return sends a value back to whoever called the function:

local function damage(base, isCritical)
    if isCritical then
        return base * 2
    end
    return base
end

local hit = damage(25, true)
print("You dealt", hit, "damage")
print("Normal hit:", damage(25, false))

A function without a return gives back nil. A function can also return several values:

local function minMax(a, b)
    if a < b then return a, b end
    return b, a
end
local low, high = minMax(9, 4)
print(low, high)

Define before you call

In Luau, a local function only exists from the line where it's written. If you call it above that line, it's still nil, and you get "attempt to call a nil value". Put your functions near the top of the script.

lessons.title: Scope and functions as values
lessons.html:
Scope

A local variable only exists inside the block where it was made: the function, loop or if statement. This is called scope.

local coins = 10            -- whole script can see this

local function addBonus()
    local bonus = 5         -- only exists inside addBonus
    coins += bonus
end

addBonus()
print(coins)                -- 15
print(bonus)                -- nil: bonus doesn't exist out here

Variables made without local are global, and they can cause hard-to-find bugs when two parts of your code use the same name. Always use local.

Functions are values

A function is a value, just like a number. You can store it in a variable or pass it to another function. A function with no name is called an anonymous function:

local function doTwice(action)
    action()
    action()
end

doTwice(function()
    print("Jump!")
end)

This is exactly how Roblox events work: you hand Roblox a function and say "run this when something happens." That's next unit!

lessons.title: Helper functions for building
lessons.html:
Functions really pay off when you build things. Instead of repeating six lines for every part, write a helper that does it and returns the new part:

local function makePart(name, position, size, color)
    local part = Instance.new("Part")
    part.Name = name
    part.Position = position
    part.Size = size
    part.Color = color
    part.Anchored = true
    part.Parent = workspace
    return part
end

makePart("Floor", Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 0), Vector3.new(20, 1, 20), Color3.fromRGB(80, 160, 80))
makePart("Wall", Vector3.new(0, 5, -10), Vector3.new(20, 10, 1), Color3.fromRGB(200, 200, 200))
local roof = makePart("Roof", Vector3.new(0, 10.5, 0), Vector3.new(22, 1, 22), Color3.fromRGB(150, 40, 40))
roof.Material = Enum.Material.Slate  -- we got the part back, so we can keep changing it

Functions + loops

Combine them for even less code. This builds a ring of pillars:

local function pillar(x, z)
    local p = Instance.new("Part")
    p.Size = Vector3.new(2, 10, 2)
    p.Position = Vector3.new(x, 5, z)
    p.Anchored = true
    p.Material = Enum.Material.Marble
    p.Parent = workspace
end

for i = 1, 12 do
    local angle = i / 12 * math.pi * 2
    pillar(math.cos(angle) * 15, math.sin(angle) * 15)
end

🛠 In Roblox Studio: organize big scripts

  1. Put helper functions at the top of the script, then the code that uses them below.
  2. Give functions verb names that say what they do: makePart, giveCoins, resetRound.
  3. When a helper is useful in many scripts, move it into a ModuleScript (Unit 12).

lessons.title: Touched events
lessons.html:
So far our scripts run from top to bottom and finish. Real games react: when a player touches lava, clicks a button or joins the game. Roblox tells your script about these moments with events.

You connect a function to an event. Roblox calls your function every time the event fires:

local p = Instance.new("Part") p.Name = "Pad" p.Anchored = true p.Size = Vector3.new(8, 1, 8) p.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 8) p.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 200, 255) p.Parent = workspace

local pad = workspace.Pad

pad.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
    print("Pad was touched by", otherPart.Name)
end)

Run it and walk your character onto the blue pad. Notice:

  • pad.Touched is the event, and :Connect(...) hooks up your function.
  • Roblox passes in the part that touched, here called otherPart. For a player, that's a body part like Left Leg.
  • It fires many times: once for each body part!

Is it a player?

A body part's Parent is the character model, and every character has a Humanoid (the thing that walks, jumps and has Health). So to check "did a player touch this?":

local p = Instance.new("Part") p.Name = "Lava" p.Anchored = true p.Size = Vector3.new(10, 1, 10) p.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 6) p.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 70, 0) p.Material = Enum.Material.Neon p.Parent = workspace

local lava = workspace.Lava

local function onTouched(otherPart)
    local character = otherPart.Parent
    local humanoid = character:FindFirstChild("Humanoid")
    if humanoid then
        humanoid.Health = 0
    end
end

lava.Touched:Connect(onTouched)

Walk onto the lava. You'll respawn a few seconds later. The if humanoid then check matters: if a falling brick touches the lava, it has no Humanoid, and without the check the script would error.

🛠 In Roblox Studio: make a kill brick

  2. Hover over the part in the Explorer, click +, and insert a Script inside the part.
  3. In that script, use local lava = script.Parent. script is the script itself, so its Parent is the Lava part.
  4. Paste the code above (without the first line) and press Play.

script.Parent in this simulator

To put a script inside a part here, add a header line like --!Script Workspace.Lava at the top. Everything below it becomes a Script inside Lava, so script.Parent works just like in Studio. You'll see this in the exercises.

lessons.title: Debounce: stop the spam
lessons.html:
Because Touched fires for every body part and keeps firing as you move, a coin that gives +1 might give +6. The fix is called a debounce: a true/false variable that blocks repeats while we're busy.

local p = Instance.new("Part") p.Name = "Button" p.Anchored = true p.Size = Vector3.new(6, 1, 6) p.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 8) p.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 200, 0) p.Parent = workspace

local button = workspace.Button
local presses = 0
local busy = false            -- the debounce

button.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
    if busy then return end   -- ignore touches while busy
    if not otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChild("Humanoid") then return end
    busy = true

    presses += 1
    print("Pressed", presses, "times")
    button.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
    task.wait(2)              -- cooldown
    button.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 200, 0)

    busy = false
end)

Try removing the if busy then return end line and stepping on the button. Watch the counter jump!

return inside the function means "stop here." Returning early is a clean way to ignore events you don't care about.

A disappearing platform

Events + waits make classic obby traps:

local p = Instance.new("Part") p.Name = "Platform" p.Anchored = true p.Size = Vector3.new(8, 1, 8) p.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, 4) p.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 220, 0) p.Parent = workspace
local s = Instance.new("Part") s.Name = "Stairs" s.Anchored = true s.Size = Vector3.new(4, 2, 4) s.Position = Vector3.new(0, 1, 12) s.Parent = workspace

local platform = workspace.Platform
local fading = false

platform.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if fading or not hit.Parent:FindFirstChild("Humanoid") then return end
    fading = true
    for i = 1, 10 do
        platform.Transparency = i / 10
        task.wait(0.1)
    end
    platform.CanCollide = false   -- now you fall through
    task.wait(3)
    platform.Transparency = 0
    platform.CanCollide = true
    fading = false
end)

lessons.title: Clicks, prompts and other events
lessons.html:
ClickDetector

Put a ClickDetector inside a part, and players can click it. Its MouseClick event tells you which player clicked:

local lamp = Instance.new("Part")
lamp.Name = "Lamp"
lamp.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
lamp.Size = Vector3.new(4, 4, 4)
lamp.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, 8)
lamp.Anchored = true
lamp.Parent = workspace

local detector = Instance.new("ClickDetector")
detector.Parent = lamp

local on = false
detector.MouseClick:Connect(function(player)
    on = not on
    lamp.Material = if on then Enum.Material.Neon else Enum.Material.Plastic
    lamp.Color = if on then Color3.fromRGB(255, 230, 120) else Color3.fromRGB(120, 120, 120)
    print(player.Name, "turned the lamp", if on then "on" else "off")
end)

Click the ball in the game view to toggle it. You need to be within 32 studs (the detector's MaxActivationDistance).

ProximityPrompt

A ProximityPrompt shows a "Press E" bubble when a player walks close. It's used for doors, shops and NPCs:

local chest = Instance.new("Part")
chest.Name = "Chest"
chest.Size = Vector3.new(4, 3, 3)
chest.Position = Vector3.new(0, 1.5, 10)
chest.Anchored = true
chest.Color = Color3.fromRGB(140, 90, 40)
chest.Material = Enum.Material.Wood
chest.Parent = workspace

local prompt = Instance.new("ProximityPrompt")
prompt.ActionText = "Open"
prompt.ObjectText = "Treasure Chest"
prompt.Parent = chest

prompt.Triggered:Connect(function(player)
    print(player.Name, "opened the chest and found 50 gold!")
    chest.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 0)
    prompt.Enabled = false
end)

Walk up to the chest and press E.

More useful events

Event Fires when
part.Touched / part.TouchEnded Something starts / stops touching the part
instance.Changed Any property changes
part:GetPropertyChangedSignal("Color") One specific property changes
folder.ChildAdded Something is put inside
humanoid.Died A character dies

:Connect returns a connection. Call connection:Disconnect() to stop listening, or use :Once(...) to listen only one time.

🛠 In Roblox Studio: add a ClickDetector

  1. Hover over a part in the Explorer, click + and add a ClickDetector.
  2. Add a Script to the same part and use script.Parent.ClickDetector.MouseClick:Connect(...).
  3. For prompts, insert a ProximityPrompt and set ActionText and HoldDuration in Properties.

lessons.title: Arrays (lists)
lessons.html:
A table is Luau's way to store many values in one variable. When the values are in order, we call it an array (or list):

local fruits = {"Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"}
print(fruits[1])      -- Apple  (arrays start at 1, not 0!)
print(fruits[3])      -- Cherry
print(#fruits)        -- 3: how many items
print(fruits[4])      -- nil: there is no 4th item

In Luau, arrays start at index 1. If you've used Python or Java, this is the big difference to remember.

Adding and removing

local queue = {"Ada", "Bob"}
table.insert(queue, "Cam")        -- add to the end
table.insert(queue, 1, "Zed")     -- add at position 1
print(table.concat(queue, ", "))  -- Zed, Ada, Bob, Cam

local first = table.remove(queue, 1)  -- remove position 1
print("Removed", first)
print(#queue, table.concat(queue, ", "))
print(table.find(queue, "Bob"))   -- where is Bob? 2

Looping through an array

local scores = {120, 85, 300, 42}

for index, score in scores do
    print(index, score)
end

local total = 0
for _, score in scores do   -- _ means "I don't need this one"
    total += score
end
print("Total:", total)

for i, v in list do goes through every item in order. You'll also see older code use for i, v in ipairs(list) do or in pairs(list). In Luau they all work for arrays.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.html:
A dictionary stores values by key (a name) instead of by position:

local sword = {
    Name = "Fire Sword",
    Damage = 25,
    Price = 150,
}

print(sword.Name)          -- Fire Sword
print(sword["Damage"])     -- same as sword.Damage
sword.Damage += 5          -- change a value
sword.Rarity = "Epic"      -- add a new key
sword.Price = nil          -- remove a key
print(sword.Damage, sword.Rarity, sword.Price)

Loop through a dictionary to see every key and value. The order is not guaranteed:

local prices = {Sword = 150, Shield = 90, Potion = 25}
for item, price in prices do
    print(item, "costs", price)
end

Tables inside tables

Most game data is tables inside tables, like a shop with many items:

local shop = {
    {Name = "Potion", Price = 25},
    {Name = "Shield", Price = 90},
    {Name = "Sword", Price = 150},
}

local coins = 100
for _, item in shop do
    if item.Price <= coins then
        print("You can afford the " .. item.Name)
    end
end

# only counts the array part of a table. For a dictionary like prices, #prices is 0, so count its keys with a loop instead.

lessons.title: Tables and the Roblox world
lessons.html:
Roblox hands you tables all the time. :GetChildren() returns an array of an object's children, which makes it easy to change many parts at once:

local f = Instance.new("Folder") f.Name = "Houses" f.Parent = workspace
for i = 1, 6 do local h = Instance.new("Part") h.Name = "House" .. i h.Anchored = true h.Size = Vector3.new(5, 5, 5) h.Position = Vector3.new(-15 + i * 6, 2.5, 0) h.Parent = f end

local palette = {
    Color3.fromRGB(255, 99, 99),
    Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 80),
    Color3.fromRGB(110, 220, 120),
    Color3.fromRGB(90, 160, 255),
}

local houses = workspace.Houses:GetChildren()
print("Found", #houses, "houses")

for _, house in houses do
    house.Color = palette[math.random(1, #palette)]
    task.wait(0.3)
end

palette[math.random(1, #palette)] is the classic way to pick a random item from a list.

Folders keep things organized

Put related parts in a Folder (like Coins or KillBricks) so your script can loop over just those. That way you can add more lava in Studio without changing your code:

for _, brick in workspace.KillBricks:GetChildren() do
    brick.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
        local humanoid = hit.Parent:FindFirstChild("Humanoid")
        if humanoid then humanoid.Health = 0 end
    end)
end

🛠 In Roblox Studio: organize with folders

  1. Right-click Workspace → Insert Object → Folder, and name it KillBricks.
  2. Drag all your lava parts into the folder in the Explorer.
  3. One script can now loop over workspace.KillBricks:GetChildren() to handle every brick.

ex.prompt:
The shop is a dictionary of item names and prices. Write two functions:

  1. priceOf(item) returns the price of that item, or nil if the shop doesn't sell it.
  2. affordable(coins) returns an array of the item names that cost coins or less. The order doesn't matter.
ex.starter:
local shop = {Sword = 150, Shield = 90, Potion = 25, Bow = 120}

local function priceOf(item)
end

	local result = {}
	-- add names to result with table.insert
	return result
end
tests: assert(priceOf("Shield") == 90, "priceOf(\"Shield\") should be 90")
assert(priceOf("Laser") == nil, "priceOf(\"Laser\") should be nil")

local shop = {Sword = 150, Shield = 90, Potion = 25, Bow = 120}

local function priceOf(item)
	return shop[item]
end

local function affordable(coins)
	local result = {}
	for name, price in shop do
		if price <= coins then
			table.insert(result, name)
		end
	end
	return result
end

lessons.title: Players and the leaderboard
lessons.html:
The Players service holds one Player object for everyone in the game. Its PlayerAdded event fires whenever someone joins, which is the perfect moment to set up their stats.

leaderstats

Roblox has a built-in leaderboard. To use it, put a Folder named exactly leaderstats inside the player, and put value objects inside it. Each IntValue, NumberValue or StringValue becomes a column:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local leaderstats = Instance.new("Folder")
    leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
    leaderstats.Parent = player

    local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
    coins.Name = "Coins"
    coins.Value = 0
    coins.Parent = leaderstats
end)

-- give everyone 1 coin every second
while true do
    task.wait(1)
    for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
        player.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 1
    end
end

Watch the leaderboard in the top-right corner count up.

  • The folder name must be lowercase leaderstats, or Roblox won't show it.
  • Value objects store their number in .Value.
  • Players:GetPlayers() returns an array of everyone in the game.

Connect before players join

PlayerAdded only fires for players who join after you connect. If your script does a long task.wait() before connecting, the first player might join before you're listening and never get stats. Connect your events at the top of the script, before any waiting.

🛠 In Roblox Studio: test with players

  1. Put leaderboard code in a Script in ServerScriptService.
  2. Press Play to test as one player. Your stats show at the top-right.
  3. To test with several players, go to the Test tab, choose 2 Players and click Start.

lessons.title: Characters and Humanoids
lessons.html:
A Player is the person. Their Character is the 3D body model in workspace. When you die and respawn, you get a brand new character, but you're the same player.

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(character)
        local humanoid = character:WaitForChild("Humanoid")
        humanoid.WalkSpeed = 30       -- default is 16
        humanoid.JumpPower = 70       -- default is 50
        print(player.Name, "spawned with super speed!")

        humanoid.Died:Connect(function()
            print(player.Name, "died. Respawning soon...")
        end)
    end)
end)

Inside every character:

Child What it is
Humanoid Controls walking and jumping. Has Health, MaxHealth, WalkSpeed, JumpPower
HumanoidRootPart The invisible center part. Move it to teleport the character
Head, Torso, arms, legs The body parts that fire Touched events

Which player touched this?

Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(model) turns a character model back into its Player. This is how you give rewards when someone touches something:

local p = Instance.new("Part") p.Name = "SpeedPad" p.Anchored = true p.Size = Vector3.new(8, 1, 8) p.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 6) p.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 140) p.Material = Enum.Material.Neon p.Parent = workspace

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local pad = workspace.SpeedPad

pad.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if player then
        hit.Parent.Humanoid.WalkSpeed = 50
        print(player.Name, "is going fast!")
    end
end)

lessons.html:
Let's combine everything into a coin you can collect for real points:

local f = Instance.new("Folder") f.Name = "Coins" f.Parent = workspace
for i = 1, 5 do local c = Instance.new("Part") c.Name = "Coin" c.Anchored = true c.CanCollide = false c.Shape = Enum.PartType.Cylinder c.Size = Vector3.new(0.6, 3, 3) c.Position = Vector3.new(-12 + i * 4, 2, 6 - i) c.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 0) c.Material = Enum.Material.Neon c.Parent = f end

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local leaderstats = Instance.new("Folder")
    leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
    leaderstats.Parent = player

    local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
    coins.Name = "Coins"
    coins.Value = 0
    coins.Parent = leaderstats
end)

for _, coin in workspace.Coins:GetChildren() do
    coin.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
        local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
        if player and coin.Parent then          -- coin.Parent is nil once destroyed
            player.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 1
            coin:Destroy()
        end
    end)
end

Checking coin.Parent is a neat debounce: after :Destroy(), the coin's Parent is nil, so extra touches do nothing.

Damage and healing

Change a Humanoid's Health to hurt or heal. humanoid:TakeDamage(10) is a handy shortcut. Health can't go above MaxHealth, and at 0 the character dies.

Checkpoints

Set player.RespawnLocation to a SpawnLocation part and the player respawns there next time they die. That's how obby checkpoints work (you'll build one in the project unit).

lessons.title: TweenService
lessons.html:
Setting Position makes a part teleport. To make it glide smoothly, use TweenService. A tween animates properties from their current values to new "goal" values over time.

local p = Instance.new("Part") p.Name = "Platform" p.Anchored = true p.Size = Vector3.new(8, 1, 8) p.Position = Vector3.new(-12, 4, 0) p.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255) p.Parent = workspace

local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local platform = workspace.Platform

local info = TweenInfo.new(
    3,                          -- seconds
    Enum.EasingStyle.Sine,      -- how it speeds up and slows down
    Enum.EasingDirection.InOut,
    -1,                         -- repeat count (-1 = forever)
    true                        -- reverse back each time
)

local goal = {Position = platform.Position + Vector3.new(24, 0, 0)}
local tween = TweenService:Create(platform, info, goal)
tween:Play()

Jump on the platform and ride it! The three steps are always the same:

  1. Make a TweenInfo (how long, what style, repeats).
  2. TweenService:Create(object, info, goalTable).
  3. Call :Play().

Tweening other properties

You can tween almost any number, Vector3, Color3 or CFrame property: Transparency, Size, Color and more. Use tween.Completed:Wait() to pause until it's finished:

local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local orb = Instance.new("Part")
orb.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
orb.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
orb.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
orb.Anchored = true
orb.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
orb.Parent = workspace

local grow = TweenService:Create(orb, TweenInfo.new(1.5, Enum.EasingStyle.Bounce), {Size = Vector3.new(8, 8, 8), Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 200)})
grow:Play()
grow.Completed:Wait()
print("Done growing!")
TweenService:Create(orb, TweenInfo.new(1), {Transparency = 1}):Play()

lessons.title: CFrame: position + rotation
lessons.html:
A part's CFrame ("coordinate frame") stores both its position and its rotation. Position is just the position part of the CFrame.

local block = Instance.new("Part")
block.Size = Vector3.new(6, 1, 2)
block.Anchored = true
block.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 120, 0)
block.Parent = workspace

-- move to (0, 5, 0) AND tilt 45 degrees around the Y axis
block.CFrame = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(45), 0)
print("Orientation:", block.Orientation)
  • CFrame.new(x, y, z) is a position with no rotation.
  • CFrame.Angles(x, y, z) is a rotation. It uses radians, so convert degrees with math.rad(degrees).
  • Multiplying CFrames combines them: first move, then rotate.

Spinning things

Multiply a part's current CFrame by a small rotation, over and over, and it spins in place:

local coin = Instance.new("Part")
coin.Shape = Enum.PartType.Cylinder
coin.Size = Vector3.new(0.6, 4, 4)
coin.Position = Vector3.new(0, 4, 0)
coin.Anchored = true
coin.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 0)
coin.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
coin.Parent = workspace

local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    coin.CFrame = coin.CFrame * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(180) * deltaTime, 0)
end)

RunService.Heartbeat fires every frame (about 60 times a second). It passes deltaTime, the seconds since the last frame. Multiplying by deltaTime makes the spin speed the same on fast and slow devices: here it's 180° per second.

Useful CFrame tools

CFrame.lookAt(from, target) A CFrame at from, facing target

part.Orientation Rotation in degrees, easy to read

lessons.title: Timers, task.spawn and day/night
lessons.html:
Doing two things at once

A while true do loop blocks the rest of the script. To run a loop in the background, wrap it in task.spawn:

task.spawn(function()
    for i = 1, 3 do
        print("Background:", i)
        task.wait(1)
    end
end)

print("This prints right away, without waiting for the loop")
task.delay(2, function()
    print("task.delay ran this 2 seconds later")
end)
Function What it does
task.wait(t) Pause this code for t seconds
task.spawn(f) Run f now, alongside the rest of the script
task.delay(t, f) Run f once, t seconds from now
time() Seconds since the game started

A day/night cycle

Lighting.ClockTime is the time of day from 0 to 24. Change it in a loop and the sky follows:

local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.ClockTime = 12

while true do
    Lighting.ClockTime += 0.1   -- wraps around after 24
    task.wait(0.05)
end

🛠 In Roblox Studio: animate with tweens in Studio

  1. Put tween scripts in the part they move, and use script.Parent.
  2. Anchored parts can be tweened. Unanchored parts are moved by physics instead, so anchor what you tween.
  3. Players standing on an anchored, tweened platform ride along with it.

lessons.title: Client vs server
lessons.html:
Roblox games are multiplayer by default. Each game runs on a Roblox server computer, and every player's device is a client connected to it.

  • Scripts (server scripts) run on the server. They control the real game: stats, damage, saving, spawning.
  • LocalScripts run on one player's device. They handle that player's screen: menus, buttons, camera, keyboard input.
  • ModuleScripts hold code that other scripts can require (Unit 12).
Put this Here Runs on
Script ServerScriptService Server
LocalScript StarterPlayer › StarterPlayerScripts Each player's device
LocalScript StarterGui (inside a ScreenGui) Each player's device
ModuleScript ReplicatedStorage (shared) or ServerStorage (server only) Whoever requires it

Never trust the client

Some players run cheat tools that change what their own device does. Anything a LocalScript decides can be faked. So important decisions happen on the server: the client can ask for something ("I want to buy a sword"), but the server checks whether it's allowed.

LocalPlayer

On a client, game.Players.LocalPlayer is the player using that device. On the server it's nil, because the server isn't a player!

Several scripts in this simulator

Write a header line to start a new script:

--!Script
print("Server: LocalPlayer is", game.Players.LocalPlayer)

--!LocalScript
local player = game.Players.LocalPlayer
print("Client: I am", player.Name)
print("Client: IsClient?", game:GetService("RunService"):IsClient())

--!Script makes a Script in ServerScriptService and --!LocalScript makes a LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts, just where you'd put them in Studio. Open the 🗂 Explorer to see them.

lessons.title: RemoteEvents
lessons.html:
Clients and the server talk using RemoteEvents. Put a RemoteEvent in ReplicatedStorage (both sides can see it), then:

Direction Sender calls Receiver listens to
Client → Server remote:FireServer(...) remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, ...) end)
Server → one client remote:FireClient(player, ...) remote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(...) end)
Server → everyone remote:FireAllClients(...) remote.OnClientEvent

Important: on the server, the first parameter of OnServerEvent is always the player who fired it. Roblox adds it automatically, so the client doesn't (and shouldn't) send it.

--!Script
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local remote = Instance.new("RemoteEvent")
remote.Name = "Greet"
remote.Parent = ReplicatedStorage

remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, message)
    print("Server got '" .. message .. "' from " .. player.Name)
    remote:FireClient(player, "Hello back, " .. player.Name .. "!")
end)

--!LocalScript
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local remote = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Greet")

remote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(reply)
    print("Client got:", reply)
end)

remote:FireServer("hi server")

The LocalScript uses WaitForChild because the RemoteEvent might not have reached the player's device yet.

Validate everything on the server

A cheater can call FireServer with any values they like. So the server must check requests:

buyRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, itemName)
    local price = PRICES[itemName]
    if not price then return end                    -- not a real item
    local coins = player.leaderstats.Coins
    if coins.Value < price then return end          -- can't afford it
    coins.Value -= price
    -- give the item...
end)

Never let the client send "how many coins to add" or "how much damage I did." Let it send what it wants to do, and let the server decide the result.

lessons.title: GUIs and keyboard input
lessons.html:
Buttons, labels and menus are GUIs. Each player has a PlayerGui folder. Anything inside a ScreenGui there is drawn on top of their screen.

--!LocalScript
local player = game.Players.LocalPlayer
local gui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
gui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local label = Instance.new("TextLabel")
label.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.4, 0.12)
label.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.3, 0.05)
label.Text = "Clicks: 0"
label.TextScaled = true
label.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(30, 30, 40)
label.TextColor3 = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
label.Parent = gui

local button = Instance.new("TextButton")
button.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.3, 0.15)
button.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.35, 0.75)
button.Text = "Click me!"
button.TextScaled = true
button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255)
button.TextColor3 = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
Instance.new("UICorner").Parent = button
button.Parent = gui

local clicks = 0
button.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function()
    clicks += 1
    label.Text = "Clicks: " .. clicks
end)

UDim2: positions on the screen

GUI sizes and positions use UDim2, which mixes a scale (a fraction of the screen) and an offset (pixels):

  • UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.1) is half the screen wide and a tenth tall. It looks the same on phones and big monitors.
  • UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50) is exactly 200 × 50 pixels.
  • UDim2.new(0.5, -100, 0, 20) mixes both: x scale, x offset, y scale, y offset.

Keyboard input

UserInputService tells a LocalScript when keys are pressed. Click the game view first, then press F or R:

--!LocalScript
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local player = game.Players.LocalPlayer

UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input, gameProcessed)
    if gameProcessed then return end   -- ignore keys typed into chat or text boxes
    if input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.F then
        print("F pressed: super jump!")
        player.Character.Humanoid.JumpPower = 120
    elseif input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.R then
        print("R pressed: normal jump")
        player.Character.Humanoid.JumpPower = 50
    end
end)

🛠 In Roblox Studio: design GUIs visually

  1. In the Explorer, add a ScreenGui to StarterGui, then add Frames, TextLabels and TextButtons inside it.
  2. Drag and resize them on screen, or set Size and Position in Properties.
  3. Add a LocalScript inside the ScreenGui. In it, script.Parent is the ScreenGui.

lessons.title: ModuleScripts
lessons.html:
As games grow, you'll want to share code and settings between many scripts. A ModuleScript is a script that returns a value (usually a table). Other scripts get that value with require.

--!ModuleScript ReplicatedStorage.GameConfig
local GameConfig = {}

GameConfig.RoundTime = 60
GameConfig.CoinValue = 5
GameConfig.Colors = {
    Red = Color3.fromRGB(255, 80, 80),
    Blue = Color3.fromRGB(80, 140, 255),
}

function GameConfig.formatTime(seconds)
    return string.format("%d:%02d", seconds // 60, seconds % 60)
end

return GameConfig

--!Script
local GameConfig = require(game.ReplicatedStorage.GameConfig)
print("Round lasts", GameConfig.formatTime(GameConfig.RoundTime))
print("Each coin is worth", GameConfig.CoinValue)

local p = Instance.new("Part")
p.Anchored = true
p.Position = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0)
p.Color = GameConfig.Colors.Blue
p.Parent = workspace

--!ModuleScript ReplicatedStorage.GameConfig makes a ModuleScript named GameConfig inside ReplicatedStorage.

  • A module runs once, the first time it's required. Every later require gets the same table back.
  • The module must end with return.
  • Modules in ReplicatedStorage can be used by both server and clients. Put secret server-only code in ServerStorage or ServerScriptService.

  2. Rename it (for example GameConfig). Studio fills in a template that returns a table.

lessons.title: Object-oriented Luau
lessons.html:
Games have lots of similar things: pets, weapons, enemies. Object-oriented programming (OOP) lets you write a "class" once and make many objects from it. Luau does this with tables and a metatable:

local Pet = {}
Pet.__index = Pet          -- objects look up missing keys (methods) in Pet

function Pet.new(name, kind)
    local self = setmetatable({}, Pet)
    self.Name = name
    self.Kind = kind
    self.Happiness = 50
    return self
end

function Pet:Feed(amount)
    self.Happiness = math.min(100, self.Happiness + amount)
    print(self.Name .. " the " .. self.Kind .. " is now at " .. self.Happiness .. " happiness")
end

local rex = Pet.new("Rex", "Dog")
local tom = Pet.new("Tom", "Cat")
rex:Feed(20)
tom:Feed(70)
rex:Feed(40)

How it works:

  • Pet.new(...) is a constructor: it builds a new table and gives it Pet as its metatable.
  • Pet.__index = Pet means: "if an object doesn't have a key (like Feed), look in Pet."
  • function Pet:Feed(amount) uses a colon, which adds a hidden first parameter called self. When you call rex:Feed(20), self is rex.

Colon vs dot

rex:Feed(20) is shorthand for Pet.Feed(rex, 20). If you accidentally write rex.Feed(20), then self becomes 20 and amount is nil, which gives a confusing error. Methods are called with :.

Classes usually live in a ModuleScript that returns the class table, so any script can require it and make objects.

lessons.title: Saving data with DataStores
lessons.html:
When a player leaves, their leaderstats are gone, unless you save them. Roblox's DataStoreService stores data online by key. A key is usually built from the player's unique UserId.

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local coinStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local leaderstats = Instance.new("Folder")
    leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
    leaderstats.Parent = player
    local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
    coins.Name = "Coins"
    coins.Parent = leaderstats

    -- LOAD
    local key = "Player_" .. player.UserId
    local success, saved = pcall(function()
        return coinStore:GetAsync(key)
    end)
    if success then
        coins.Value = saved or 0     -- saved is nil for brand-new players
        print("Loaded", coins.Value, "coins")
    else
        warn("Couldn't load data:", saved)
    end

    -- earn a coin every second so there's something to save
    while player.Parent do
        task.wait(1)
        coins.Value += 1
    end
end)

-- SAVE
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    local key = "Player_" .. player.UserId
    local success, err = pcall(function()
        coinStore:SetAsync(key, player.leaderstats.Coins.Value)
    end)
    print(if success then "Saved!" else "Save failed: " .. tostring(err))
end)

Run it, wait a few seconds, press ■ Stop (that's like leaving the game), then Run again. Your coins come back! This simulator saves DataStores in your browser so you can practice.

Why pcall?

DataStore calls go over the internet, so they can fail. pcall(fn) ("protected call") runs a function and catches errors instead of crashing the script. It returns true plus the results, or false plus the error message.

local ok, result = pcall(function()
    error("the server is busy")
end)
print(ok, result)

DataStore tips

  • Don't save too often. Save when a player leaves (plus maybe every few minutes), not every time a coin changes.
  • Use UpdateAsync when the new value depends on the old one.
  • Use game:BindToClose(function() ... end) to save everyone when a server shuts down.
  • You can save numbers, strings, booleans and tables of those, but not Instances like Parts.

🛠 In Roblox Studio: turn on DataStores

  1. Publish your place: File → Publish to Roblox.
  2. Open Game Settings → Security and turn on Enable Studio Access to API Services.
  3. Now DataStores work when you press Play in Studio. (Use a separate test place so you don't mess up real players' data.)

ex.prompt:
Make a class called Account:

  • Account.new(owner, balance) creates an account.
  • account:Deposit(amount) adds money.
  • account:Withdraw(amount) removes money and returns true, but if there isn't enough it changes nothing and returns false.
  • account:GetBalance() returns the balance.

	-- store owner and balance
	return self

local a = Account.new("Ada", 50) assert(a:Withdraw(20) == true and a:GetBalance() == 30, "Withdrawing 20 from 50 should return true and leave 30")

ex.solution:
local Account = {}
Account.__index = Account

function Account.new(owner, balance)
	local self = setmetatable({}, Account)
	self.Owner = owner
	self.Balance = balance
	return self
end

function Account:Deposit(amount)
	self.Balance += amount
end

function Account:Withdraw(amount)
	if amount > self.Balance then
		return false
	end
	self.Balance -= amount
	return true
end

function Account:GetBalance()
	return self.Balance
end

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)

	leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
	leaderstats.Parent = player
	local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
	coins.Name = "Coins"
	coins.Parent = leaderstats

	local ok, saved = pcall(function()
		return store:GetAsync("Player_" .. player.UserId)

lessons.title: Project 1: Build an obby
lessons.html:
Time to build real games! An obby (obstacle course) uses almost everything you've learned. Here's a complete mini-obby. Run it and try to beat it, then read the code.

local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local course = Instance.new("Folder")
course.Name = "Obby"
course.Parent = workspace

local function block(name, pos, size, color, material)
    local p = Instance.new("Part")
    p.Name = name
    p.Position = pos
    p.Size = size
    p.Color = color
    p.Material = material or Enum.Material.Plastic
    p.Anchored = true
    p.Parent = course
    return p
end

-- 1. Stepping stones
for i = 1, 4 do
    block("Stone", Vector3.new(0, 1 + i, 14 - i * 6), Vector3.new(4, 1, 4), Color3.fromHSV(i / 8, 0.6, 1))
end

-- 2. Kill bricks under a narrow bridge
block("Bridge", Vector3.new(0, 5, -16), Vector3.new(2, 1, 10), Color3.fromRGB(200, 200, 200))
local lava = block("Lava", Vector3.new(0, 0.5, -16), Vector3.new(16, 1, 12), Color3.fromRGB(255, 70, 0), Enum.Material.Neon)
lava.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local humanoid = hit.Parent:FindFirstChild("Humanoid")
    if humanoid then humanoid.Health = 0 end
end)

-- 3. A moving platform
local mover = block("Mover", Vector3.new(-6, 5, -26), Vector3.new(5, 1, 5), Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255))
TweenService:Create(mover, TweenInfo.new(2, Enum.EasingStyle.Sine, Enum.EasingDirection.InOut, -1, true),
    {Position = Vector3.new(6, 5, -26)}):Play()

-- 4. The win pad
local win = block("WinPad", Vector3.new(0, 5, -36), Vector3.new(8, 1, 8), Color3.fromRGB(80, 255, 120), Enum.Material.Neon)
local winners = {}
win.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if player and not winners[player] then
        winners[player] = true
        print("🏆 " .. player.Name .. " beat the obby!")
    end
end)

How it's built

  • A helper function (block) builds every part, so each obstacle is one line.
  • A for loop makes the stepping stones.
  • Touched + Humanoid makes the lava deadly.
  • TweenService moves the platform. Players riding it move along.
  • A dictionary (winners[player] = true) remembers who already won, so the message prints once per player.

Checkpoints

In a real obby, dying sends you back to your last checkpoint, not the start. Make each checkpoint a SpawnLocation, and when a player touches it, set player.RespawnLocation to it. Add a Stage stat to leaderstats so players can see their progress.

🎯 Your turn: Copy this obby into Roblox Studio, then make it yours. Add a spinning bar to jump over (CFrame + Heartbeat), a disappearing platform (Unit 7), and checkpoints with a Stage stat (the exercise below).

lessons.title: Project 2: Coin rush
lessons.html:
A round-based game has a timer, a goal and a winner. In Coin Rush, coins rain down for 30 seconds and players collect as many as they can.

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ROUND_TIME = 30

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local leaderstats = Instance.new("Folder")
    leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
    leaderstats.Parent = player
    local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
    coins.Name = "Coins"
    coins.Parent = leaderstats
end)

local coinFolder = Instance.new("Folder")
coinFolder.Name = "Coins"
coinFolder.Parent = workspace

local function spawnCoin()
    local coin = Instance.new("Part")
    coin.Name = "Coin"
    coin.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
    coin.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
    coin.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 0)
    coin.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
    coin.Position = Vector3.new(math.random(-25, 25), 25, math.random(-25, 15))
    coin.Parent = coinFolder   -- not anchored, so it falls!

    coin.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
        local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
        if player and coin.Parent then
            player.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 1
            coin:Destroy()
        end
    end)
end

task.wait(2)
print("Round starting!")
for timeLeft = ROUND_TIME, 1, -1 do
    if timeLeft % 5 == 0 then print(timeLeft .. " seconds left") end
    spawnCoin()
    task.wait(1)
end

coinFolder:ClearAllChildren()
for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
    print(player.Name .. " collected " .. player.Leaderstats.Coins.Value .. " coins!")
end

There's a bug at the very end: run the game until the round is over and read the red error. Can you fix it? (Hint: Unit 9's bug hunt.)

Make it better

  • Show the time left on a TextLabel using a RemoteEvent or a StringValue the client watches.
  • Make rare golden coins worth 5: if math.random() < 0.1 then.
  • Loop the whole round with while true do ... end and an intermission.
  • Reset everyone's Coins to 0 at the start of each round.

lessons.title: Project 3: Clicker simulator
lessons.html:
Simulator games are all about numbers going up. This one uses every big idea from the course: GUIs, RemoteEvents, server validation and leaderstats.

--!Script
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local clickRemote = Instance.new("RemoteEvent")
clickRemote.Name = "Click"
clickRemote.Parent = ReplicatedStorage
local upgradeRemote = Instance.new("RemoteEvent")
upgradeRemote.Name = "Upgrade"
upgradeRemote.Parent = ReplicatedStorage

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local ls = Instance.new("Folder")
    ls.Name = "leaderstats"
    ls.Parent = player
    local clicks = Instance.new("IntValue")
    clicks.Name = "Clicks"
    clicks.Parent = ls
    local power = Instance.new("IntValue")
    power.Name = "Power"
    power.Value = 1
    power.Parent = ls
end)

local lastClick = {}
clickRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player)
    -- anti-cheat: no more than 20 clicks per second
    local now = time()
    if lastClick[player] and now - lastClick[player] < 0.05 then return end
    lastClick[player] = now
    player.leaderstats.Clicks.Value += player.leaderstats.Power.Value
end)

upgradeRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player)
    local ls = player.leaderstats
    local cost = ls.Power.Value * 10
    if ls.Clicks.Value >= cost then
        ls.Clicks.Value -= cost
        ls.Power.Value += 1
    end
end)

--!LocalScript
local player = game.Players.LocalPlayer
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local clickRemote = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Click")
local upgradeRemote = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Upgrade")
local power = player:WaitForChild("leaderstats"):WaitForChild("Power")

local gui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
gui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local function makeButton(text, y, color)
    local b = Instance.new("TextButton")
    b.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.34, 0.16)
    b.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.33, y)
    b.BackgroundColor3 = color
    b.TextColor3 = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
    b.TextScaled = true
    b.Text = text
    Instance.new("UICorner").Parent = b
    b.Parent = gui
    return b
end

local clickButton = makeButton("CLICK!", 0.55, Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255))
local upgradeButton = makeButton("", 0.76, Color3.fromRGB(255, 140, 0))

local function refresh()
    upgradeButton.Text = "Upgrade (" .. power.Value * 10 .. " clicks)"
end
refresh()
power.Changed:Connect(refresh)

clickButton.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function() clickRemote:FireServer() end)
upgradeButton.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function() upgradeRemote:FireServer() end)

Click away and watch your stats on the leaderboard. Notice:

  • The client only asks ("I clicked", "I want to upgrade"). The server decides how many clicks you get and whether you can afford an upgrade.
  • The server ignores clicks that come in impossibly fast (a simple rate limit).
  • The upgrade cost lives on the server, so a cheater can't make upgrades free.

🎯 Your turn: Add saving with a DataStore (Unit 12), a Rebirth button that resets Clicks and Power but gives a permanent multiplier, and a sound or color flash on each click.

lessons.title: Publishing and what's next
lessons.html:
Publish your game

🛠 In Roblox Studio: share your game with friends

  1. File → Publish to Roblox. Give it a name and description.
  2. Open Game Settings → Permissions and set it to Public when you're ready.
  3. Add an icon and thumbnails on the Creator Dashboard (create.roblox.com).
  4. Playtest with friends using Test → Start with several players, then on real devices (phone, tablet, PC).

A checklist for your scripts

  • Important logic (stats, damage, purchases) runs on the server.
  • Every RemoteEvent handler validates what the client sends.
  • Every while true do loop has a task.wait().
  • Touched events have a debounce.
  • Variables are local, and names explain what they hold.
  • DataStore calls are wrapped in pcall and you save on PlayerRemoving and BindToClose.
  • Use :WaitForChild() in LocalScripts.

Where to go next

  • Roblox Creator Hub (create.roblox.com/docs): the official guides and the full reference for every class, property and event.
  • Developer Forum (devforum.roblox.com): ask questions and read community tutorials.
  • luau.org: the language reference, including type annotations like local speed: number = 16, which help catch bugs early.
  • Explore more services: Sound, ParticleEmitter, PathfindingService (NPCs that walk around obstacles), Raycast (lasers and line-of-sight), and CollectionService (tagging objects).

You now know the core of Roblox scripting: Instances and properties, events, players, tweens, client/server networking, modules, OOP and saving data. Go make something fun! 🎮

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	local ls = Instance.new("Folder")
	ls.Name = "leaderstats"
	ls.Parent = player
	local stage = Instance.new("IntValue")
	stage.Name = "Stage"
	stage.Value = 0
	stage.Parent = ls
end)

for _, checkpoint in workspace.Checkpoints:GetChildren() do
	checkpoint.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
		local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
		if not player then return end
		local number = tonumber(checkpoint.Name)
		local stage = player.leaderstats.Stage
		if number > stage.Value then
			stage.Value = number
			player.RespawnLocation = checkpoint
		end
	end)
end

ex.solution:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local click = Instance.new("RemoteEvent")
click.Name = "Click"
click.Parent = ReplicatedStorage
local upgrade = Instance.new("RemoteEvent")
upgrade.Name = "Upgrade"
upgrade.Parent = ReplicatedStorage

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	local ls = Instance.new("Folder")
	ls.Name = "leaderstats"
	ls.Parent = player
	local clicks = Instance.new("IntValue")
	clicks.Name = "Clicks"
	clicks.Parent = ls
	local power = Instance.new("IntValue")
	power.Name = "Power"
	power.Value = 1
	power.Parent = ls
end)

click.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player)
	local ls = player.leaderstats
	ls.Clicks.Value += ls.Power.Value
end)

upgrade.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player)
	local ls = player.leaderstats
	local cost = ls.Power.Value * 10
	if ls.Clicks.Value >= cost then
		ls.Clicks.Value -= cost
		ls.Power.Value += 1
	end
end)
